migrationNotes: SPINE: Start from one text message and follow the gap between its two halves: try a full stop, a comma with a conjunction, a semicolon, a colon and a dash in turn, and see what each one tells the reader about how the halves belong together.

lesson.title: Joining two clauses

lead.text: Two complete statements side by side raise a small problem, because the writer must decide what goes between them. Each is an independent clause, in the last lesson's words, so each could stand as a sentence. “The shop closed” is one and “We went home” is another.

The plainest choice is a full stop: “The shop closed. We went home.” The reader gets two sentences and works out the connection alone. To make one sentence, the writer needs a joiner. The usual one is a comma followed by a coordinating conjunction, a short word that links clauses of equal weight, such as “and”, “but”, “so”, “or” and “yet”. Each names a relation. “And” adds. “But” sets one against the other. “So” gives a result.

afterFigure.text: A comma on its own is too light for the job. “The shop closed, we went home” runs two complete statements together with nothing but a comma between them. Editors call this a comma splice, and in formal writing it counts as an error. Some writers splice on purpose. Frederick Douglass told a Fourth of July audience in Rochester in 1852, “You may rejoice, I must mourn”. The abruptness makes the two fates collide.

lead.text: Back to the message in the opening.
Here is a sentence with only a comma between its halves.

reveal.text: You named the fault. A writer who splices deliberately, as Douglass does, is breaking the rule with a purpose. A writer who splices by accident is simply making an error.

lead.text: A semicolon offers a second way to join two complete statements. It does the joining by itself, so no conjunction is needed: “The hall emptied; the street filled.” The mark tells the reader that the two statements are one thought, and the reader supplies the connection. It suits a link that is clear without a word to spell it out.

Both sides of a semicolon must be able to stand as sentences. “The hall emptied; because the lights went out” fails, since the words after the mark cannot stand alone. The semicolon follows the same rule as the full stop, with a whole clause on each side.

afterFigure.text: The second case shows what a semicolon makes possible. In “Alice chose tea; Ben, coffee; Carol, juice” the second and third clauses have no verb. The reader borrows “chose” from the first clause, and a comma marks the gap where the verb was left out. Because commas are already busy inside each clause, the semicolons keep the clauses apart.

steps.headline: Repair “The rain stopped, the match began” in two ways.

lead.text: Two of the fixes from the last screens, applied to one splice.

workedSteps.text: Check each side. “The rain stopped” and “the match began” are both full clauses, so a comma alone cannot join them.
Option one: swap the comma for a semicolon. “The rain stopped; the match began.”
Option two: keep the comma and add a conjunction that fits. “The rain stopped, so the match began.”

steps.headline: Find the verb Douglass leaves out of his second and third clauses.

lead.text: Douglass joins three charges with semicolons. The second and third are shorter than the first.

reveal.text: The comma marks where the verb was dropped. Commas inside each clause are already busy, so the semicolons separate the clauses.

workedSteps.text: Read the first clause whole: “To him, your celebration is a sham;”
The second clause has a subject, “your boasted liberty”, and a complement, “an unholy license”, but no verb.
Which verb from the first clause is understood here?

steps.headline: A mark that promises an explanation

lead.text: The colon works differently from the semicolon. It follows a complete statement and makes a promise: what comes next will explain or spell out what you have just read. “The reason was simple: the bridge was closed.” The first part could stand alone, and the second part says what the simple reason was.

Shakespeare uses a colon this way at the end of line 2 of Sonnet 18. He tells the beloved that they are more lovely and more temperate, and the lines that follow set out why summer falls short. The test is the same as for the semicolon. The words before a colon must be able to stand as a sentence.

afterFigure.text: A colon fits when the second part answers the question that the first part raises. When the second part only adds another fact, a semicolon or a conjunction suits better.

lead.text: Three sentences use a colon. Test the words before each one.

reveal.text: You tested the words before each colon. Only a complete clause can make the promise that the second part keeps.

lead.text: You now have several ways to join the same pair of clauses, and each says something different. A comma with a conjunction names the relation. A semicolon says the clauses are one thought and leaves the relation to the reader. A colon says the second clause explains the first.

A dash is the sharpest of these. It breaks the sentence and makes the reader stop. Lincoln's Bliss copy of the Gettysburg Address uses dashes to hold “we can not dedicate” apart from “we can not consecrate”, so that each verb lands harder than the one before.

afterFigure.text: Choose by asking what you want the reader to know. A conjunction suits a relation that matters, a semicolon suits two statements that simply belong together, and a colon suits a second statement that explains the first.

lead.text: One sentence can use several of these marks, and the count from the last lesson still works. Find each subject with its finite verb, then ask whether that clause could stand alone. “The ferry was cancelled; the crowd waited: the next boat was due at noon” has three independent clauses, one before each mark and one at the end.

A dependent clause does not add to the count of independent clauses. In “The ferry was cancelled because the wind rose; the crowd waited”, the clause opened by “because” leans on the first clause, so the sentence has two independent clauses and one dependent clause.

afterFigure.text: The marks do not change the count. A semicolon, a colon or a conjunction sits between complete clauses, and each complete clause with its own finite verb is one more to count.

lead.text: A comma splice has more than one repair. Here the second clause is the result of the first.

reveal.text: The second clause is the result of the first, so the conjunction names the relation that the comma left out.

lesson.orientation: Repair a comma splice and choose between a semicolon, a colon, a dash and a conjunction by what each mark says about the relation.
lesson.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh text after a delay.

blocks.text: You are texting a friend about last night. You waited at the stop and the bus never came, and you want to say so in one sentence. You type “We waited, the bus never came” and press send. The message reads perfectly well.

Put the same words in an essay and an editor will circle the comma. The words are identical, so the trouble lies in what a comma can carry. The marks between two statements do real work. A full stop, a comma, a semicolon and a colon each tell the reader something different about how the statements fit together, and a writer who chooses well says more than one who chooses by habit.
This lesson takes plain statements and tries each mark between them in turn. You will see which joins hold and which fail, and what the good ones say.

diagram.caption: The same two statements with a different mark between them. The rest of the lesson looks at what each mark tells the reader.

intro.promise: By the end you'll join two clauses cleanly and say what each mark tells the reader about how they relate.

recap.keyIdea: A comma alone cannot join two independent clauses. Choose a semicolon, a colon, a dash or a conjunction by the relation you mean.

blocks.text: You split the bus message into its two sentences, named the comma splice and repaired one with “so”. You also read the verb Douglass leaves out between his semicolons, tested a colon, and counted three clauses in a sentence that uses two different marks.

recap.nextHook: Clauses are only as strong as the subjects and verbs inside them, and the next lesson begins with a smashed shop window and a member of staff who would rather not say who did it.

questions.prompt: 'The vote was close, the motion failed.' Two independent clauses are joined by a comma alone. What do editors call this construction?
hints: Look at what separates the two halves, and at whether each half could stand alone.
The name pairs the mark with a word from rope-work and film editing.
Joining two lengths of rope or film end to end is called splicing.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A comma splice: in edited prose a comma alone cannot join two independent clauses.

questions.onCorrect: A comma splice: a comma alone cannot join two independent clauses in edited prose.

misconceptions.feedback: A run-on has no punctuation at all between the clauses. Here a comma is present.
A fragment lacks a subject or a verb. Both halves here are complete clauses.

questions.prompt: Douglass: 'To him, your celebration is a sham; your boasted liberty, an unholy license; your national greatness, swelling vanity.' Which verb is understood but not repeated in the second and third clauses?
hints: Read the first clause, then lend its verb to the second.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: 'Is': each later clause means 'your boasted liberty is an unholy license'. The comma marks where the verb was left out.

questions.onCorrect: “Is” is understood in the later clauses. The comma marks the gap where it was left out.

misconceptions.feedback: That is a subject or a complement, not a verb. Find the verb the first clause lends to the others.
The missing verb is borrowed from the first clause exactly as it stands there.

questions.prompt: Which sentence uses the colon correctly?
hints: Test the words before each colon: could they stand as a sentence?

acceptedIdeas: The verdict was clear: the motion had failed by two votes.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A colon needs a complete clause before it, and what follows should explain or specify. Only the first sentence meets both conditions.

choices.label: The verdict was clear: the motion had failed by two votes.
The motion: failed by two votes.
The reasons were: cost and delay.

questions.onCorrect: A colon needs a full clause before it, and what follows should explain it. Only this sentence meets both.

misconceptions.feedback: Test the words before the colon: “The motion” cannot stand as a sentence.
“The reasons were” cannot stand as a sentence, so a colon after it is misplaced.

questions.prompt: Repair 'It was late, we left' by keeping the comma and adding a coordinating conjunction that states cause and result. Which conjunction do you add?
hints: The second clause is the result of the first. Which short word introduces a result?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: 'So': 'It was late, so we left.' 'And' would join the clauses without naming the cause.

questions.onCorrect: “So” names the result. “It was late, so we left” says why they left, which “and” would not.

misconceptions.feedback: “And” only adds a second fact. Ask how the second clause relates to the first.
“But” signals contrast. Here the second clause follows from the first.
“Because” opens a dependent clause and would not follow a comma here. Use a coordinating conjunction.

questions.prompt: Douglass writes 'You may rejoice, I must mourn.' Keeping the comma, which coordinating conjunction would make this standard edited prose while keeping the contrast?
hints: Choose the conjunction that sets one clause against the other.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: 'But' or 'yet': 'You may rejoice, but I must mourn.' Both name the contrast; 'and' would flatten it.

questions.onCorrect: “But” sets one clause against the other. “Yet” does the same job.

misconceptions.feedback: “And” would flatten the contrast into a plain addition.
“So” gives a result, and rejoicing does not cause mourning.

questions.prompt: How many independent clauses are in 'The hall was full; the speaker was late: his train had stopped outside the city.'?
hints: Find each subject with its finite verb.
Check whether any clause opens with a subordinator such as 'because' or 'when'.
Each mark here separates complete clauses.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Three: 'The hall was full', 'the speaker was late' and 'his train had stopped outside the city'. The colon introduces the reason for the lateness.

questions.onCorrect: Three: each of the three clauses has its own subject and verb, and the marks separate them.

misconceptions.feedback: Two is close. Check the part after the colon: it is a full clause too.
Each mark here separates complete clauses, so there is more than one.
Count only subject-and-verb pairs, and check that each could stand as a sentence.

questions.prompt: The message reads “We waited, the bus never came”. Split it into the fewest complete sentences. How many sentences do you get?
hints: Read each half of the comma aloud on its own.
Does each half make sense standing alone?
Count the halves that could be sentences.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Two: “We waited.” and “The bus never came.”

questions.onCorrect: Two. Each half is a full clause that could stand alone, and a comma is too weak to join them.

misconceptions.feedback: A comma does not make one sentence out of two. Try reading each half on its own.
Each half is already a complete sentence. You do not need to split further.

questions.prompt: Which mark links two clauses as one thought, without a conjunction?
hints: Think of the mark that sits between a comma and a full stop in strength.
questions.onCorrect: A semicolon links two full clauses as one thought and leaves their relation unstated.

misconceptions.feedback: A comma on its own is too weak to hold two full clauses.
A full stop keeps the clauses apart. The question asks for a mark that links them.

questions.prompt: Why does the semicolon need no conjunction here?

acceptedIdeas: It already links two full clauses as one thought.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A semicolon links two complete clauses without a conjunction.

choices.label: It already links two full clauses as one thought.
It is just a heavier comma.

questions.onCorrect: A semicolon is a full link between clauses: it joins them without saying how they relate.

misconceptions.feedback: A comma cannot do this job, so the semicolon is not just a stronger version of it.
Semicolons do separate list items that contain commas, but they also join clauses.

questions.prompt: Which sentence uses a semicolon correctly?
hints: Check that each side of the semicolon could stand as a sentence.

acceptedIdeas: The match was cancelled; the pitch was flooded.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The match was cancelled; the pitch was flooded.

choices.label: The match was cancelled; the pitch was flooded.
The match was cancelled; because the pitch was flooded.

questions.onCorrect: Both halves are full clauses, so a semicolon can join them without a conjunction.

misconceptions.feedback: “Because the pitch was flooded” cannot stand alone, so a semicolon cannot join it.
The words before the semicolon are not a full clause. A semicolon needs complete clauses on both sides.
